newsitem.title: FRANCE: If French voters take a hard left, Hue is waiting.
newsitem.headline: If French voters take a hard left, Hue is waiting.

text.p: When President Jacques Chirac decided to dissolve parliament and call an early French election, Communist party boss Robert Hue received the courtesy telephone call before Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin.

Hue tells the anecdote with far more humour than malice, but is also making an important political point, that the Communist party is a force to be reckoned with, not just by the right, but by his party's far larger Socialist rivals.

He feels the Communists are in with a chance, the chance of tugging left-wing voters distinctly to the left and giving his party genuine political leverage if the electorate swings away from the right in the two-stage parlimamentrary election being held on May 25 and June 1.
Heading for a campaign rally in this Mediterranean port on Tuesday, Hue had used his flight time to spell out to reporters his ambition of a "strong left" alternative.

His party has struck a pact with the Socialists, but it is not a joint programme for government and he hopes traditional militancy will turn into further gains and greater weight for the Communists in the closing stages of the campaign.

The first voting day is less than three weeks away, but even if opinion polls predict victory for the centre-right coalition, they show a far slimmer majority over the combined Socialist and Communist vote.

The polls show the Socialists winning up to 30 percent of votes and the Communists around 10 percent, neck-and-neck with the ruling RPR/UDF coalition but the pollsters see the coalition winning a majority of about 50 seats in the National Assembly.
"There's not a single poll which shows the Socialists getting enough without us," Hue said. He said private soundings of voters comforted his hopes the party could gain 12 percent.

Hue, a squat judo expert who combines rousing rhetoric at public rallies with cheerful combat in television debate, says there is no point in hiding differences with Lionel Jospin's Socialists, most fundamentally over Europe.

He regrets that Chirac opted for an election 10 months ahead of schedule but says he is surprised by the ease with which the Communists and Socialists rose to the challenge. "Chirac didn't think we could make the sauce come together," Hue says.

Hue openly admits that his party has not bridged a gap with the Socialists on issues as crucial as Communist opposition to the planned European single currency, but says the centre-right is far from united and dismisses its RPR/UDF joint manifesto.
"We're just a little less pretentious about victory, flexing the muscles" he quips.
Asked how would Communists and Socialists might work together on Europe, Hue suggests the euro might not materialise. "I just don't think it's going to happen. Let's wait and see."

At his Marseille speech Hue hammers out his call to reject government spending cuts and austerity, and accuses the extreme-right National Front of trying to steal ground in working class areas "when it is the party of the millionaire (Jean Marie) Le Pen".

"Voting Communist means saying a loud and clear 'No' to this devastating cult of 'King Money', 'No' to a system where the law of financial profit runs roughshod over people's dignity, where politicial sleaze holds sway and throws human beings around like merchandise," Hue told several thousand supporters.

His alternative is to boost consumption to promote economic growth by cutting indirect taxes like value-added tax, cutting working hours, creating 1.5 million jobs and hiking taxes on the rich, on companies and on financial markets.

Beyond the fervour of political rallies, Hue goes to pains to point out that he is anything but a traditional apparatchik and that he has "abolsutely no accounts to settle" with the past as the party pulls through the demise of the Communist bloc.
"My entire party experience is as an elected representative, not as part of the aparatus," says Hue, the first French Communist leader born after World War Two.
"I'm a Marxist, but....," and he falls into silence.
